desc:
The array nums is sorted in strictly increasing order. Build a height-balanced binary search tree that stores exactly these values (in a height-balanced tree the left and right subtrees of every node differ in height by at most one), and return it in level-order encoding.

Many balanced trees exist, so to make the answer unique use this rule: for any range of the array, the root is the lower middle element, that is the element at index (lo + hi) / 2 rounded down, where lo and hi are the first and last index of the range. The elements to its left form the left subtree and those to its right form the right subtree, built with the same rule.

Tree encoding. A binary tree is written as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (real node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [5,2,7,-1,3,6] is the tree whose root 5 has left child 2 and right child 7; node 2 has no left child and right child 3; node 7 has left child 6 and no right child.

Example 1

nums = [1,2,3,4,5]
Output: [3,1,4,-1,2,-1,5]
Root 3; the left range [1,2] has lower middle 1 (child 2 on its right); the right range [4,5] has lower middle 4 (child 5 on its right).

Example 2

nums = [10,20]
Output: [10,-1,20]
hints: A binary search tree read in inorder gives a sorted list, so the array is exactly the inorder sequence of the tree you must build.
To keep the tree balanced, the root should split the remaining elements into two parts of (almost) equal size. Which element does that?

Take the middle index of the range as the root, then build the left subtree from the part before it and the right subtree from the part after it. Finally write the tree level by level; recursion depth is only O(log n), or use an explicit stack.
editorial: Choosing the middle element as root puts about half of the values in each subtree, and repeating this rule inside each subtree keeps the sizes of the two sides within one of each other, so heights differ by at most one everywhere. The ordering holds automatically: everything left of the middle is smaller, everything right of it is larger.

Implement it by working on index ranges rather than slicing the array (slicing copies and costs O(n log n)). Every element becomes a node exactly once, so building is O(n). Producing the level-order output is another O(n) pass with a queue. The tree has height about log<sub>2</sub> n, so a recursive version is safe.
